name: Dun
summary: Dun is a coat dilution controlled by regulatory variants at TBX3 on chromosome 8, with three alleles in one dominance order: D over nd1 over nd2 (the ids here are D, d1 and d2). D, the ancestral allele, lightens both red and black pigment on the body while largely sparing the head, lower legs, mane and tail, and adds darker primitive markings: a dorsal stripe and, variably, leg bars, shoulder stripes, a face mask and cobwebbing on the forehead. It gives red dun on a chestnut, bay dun on a bay and grullo on a black. One copy is enough, and two copies look no different. nd1 does not dilute but may still show primitive markings; it differs from D by one base, G>T, 1,066 bases into a 1.6 kb regulatory sequence downstream of TBX3 (written chr8:18,227,267+1,066G>T on EquCab2.0; on EquCab3.0 OMIA gives the nd1 haplotype as NC_009151.3:g.[20665796_20665797insCCTTCTGGC;20665807_20665808ins[1610]]); nd2, a 1,617 base-pair deletion of that same sequence, neither dilutes nor marks. So primitive markings alone do not prove a horse is dun. The dilution comes from pigment being laid down unevenly within each hair. The non-dun alleles change where and how much TBX3 is expressed in the hair follicle and leave the protein intact. D and nd1 both predate domestication; nd2 is thought to be more recent, and most modern domestic horses are non-dun. Dun is described as frequent in Nordic ponies, Highland Ponies, Icelandic Horses, Koniks, Przewalski-derived populations and many draft and pony breeds, and rare or absent in many hot-blooded breeds; no per-breed figure was given. No effect on build, performance or health is established.

alleles.name: Non-dun 1 (nd1; G>T in the 1.6 kb sequence below TBX3)

phenotypes.name: Non-dun, unmarked
phenotypes.description: No dilution and no primitive markings from this locus. A dorsal stripe can still appear through countershading, which is not this locus.

phenotypes.name: Non-dun, may show primitive markings
phenotypes.description: No dilution: the horse is its base colour. It may still show a dorsal stripe, leg barring and other primitive markings, though not every such horse does; a horse with two nd1 copies may show them more consistently than one with nd1 and nd2, which has not been measured. nd1 is dominant over nd2, so one copy is enough.

phenotypes.name: Dun
phenotypes.description: Both red and black pigment are lightened on the body, while the head, lower legs, mane and tail are largely spared. A chestnut becomes a sandy red dun with a more saturated mane and tail, a bay becomes a bay dun with dark points, and a black becomes a slate or mouse-grey grullo. Darker primitive markings come with it - a dorsal stripe and, variably, leg bars, shoulder stripes, a face mask and cobwebbing on the forehead - and their strength and completeness differ from horse to horse. One D copy gives the whole effect; two copies look the same.
